body:
Paragraph 34-
>History shows that leisured aristocracies tend to become decadent.
>  This is not true of fighting aristocracies that have to struggle to
>  maintain their power.
>  But leisured, secure aristocracies that have no need to exert themselves
>  usually become bored, hedonistic and demoralized, even though they have
>  power.

For a long time, I have thought that modern workers are the equivalent of the
serfs of the middle ages. Free, but not really. Most people are only a few
paychecks away from homelessness, unless they dig into their retirement plans,
(and postpone poverty). It's interesting to extend the analogy, because it
makes more sense, when one thinks of corporations as the new "fighting
aristocracies". There is no more (or as much) sense in one corporation
challenging another than, for example, there was for Henry VIII's invasion of
France (and for a while, parts of modern day France belonged to England), etc.,
etc, and so forth. In the middle ages, it was for glory and additions to the
treasury. Today, it is for profit and whatever corporate pride is politically
correct. We wonder about the wars of invasion of the middle ages, as though we
are superior, and think our predecessors were being foolish in supporting these
campaigns. How are we different?

In a way, not much, I think. But we could be different, in looking at
alternatives to the lifestyle prescribed by big business and its advertisers,
and by questioning our own daily decisions. Speak your mind, to your friends,
to your representatives. Join groups that you agree with, and participate in
their activism. Tell your boss that he may be wrong about something you
disagree with (politely, of course). Evaluate your choices. Don't let up if you
get rebuffed, just try a different tactic. Don't buy something you don't need -
you may not really want it! Walk instead of driving, if it's not too far. This
may reek a bit of reform, but I also think that it represents personal action.

Of course, even back then, there were resistors. They were scared too, but
thought they could make a difference. However, in this corporation/consumer
oriented world, I think that we have more chance of creating change, in favor
of the people, than ever before. But only if we act.

Susan
